newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan private sector faces credit squeeze.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan private sector faces credit squeeze.

text.p: Pakistan's private sector has been hit by a credit squeeze arising from government efforts to slash its budget deficit to meet conditions set by the International Monetary Fund, analysts said on Wednesday.
"The current credit squeeze is likely to continue at least till June," said analyst Raza Mirza of KASB & Co Ltd.
The government has tightened credit as part of an IMF-agreed drive to cut its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from 6.3 percent in the 1995/96 (July-June) financial year.

A State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) official said the central bank had siphoned off 164 billion rupees ($4.08 billion) in open market operations and auctioned 107 billion rupees worth of T-bills, replaced by short-term federal bonds in July, in calendar 1996.
He said the central bank and the government had extracted 271 billion rupees from the banking system in 1996.

High public borrowing pushed up annual yields on six-month short-term federal bonds during the year. The yield reached 17.25 percent at one open market operation on December 24, when the SBP picked up 2.18 billion rupees, the official said.
The weighted average yield on treasury bills ranged from about 12.6 percent to 13 percent in fiscal 1995/96.
Overnight interbank rates have hovered around 20 percent, the same as the SBP discount rate, but jumped to 23 percent a few days ago in a cash-short market, the official said.
One banker said banks had discounted some 12 billion rupees from the SBP on Sunday to meet their liquidity needs, but the central bank has not confirmed the amount.
Mirza said the credit squeeze would have no direct impact on inflation, which would remain high but flat.
The consumer price index, widely believed to understate inflation, rose 11.41 percent year-on-year in December compared to 11.18 percent in November and 12.34 percent in December 1995.
One casualty of tight credit has been the cotton trade, the backbone of Pakistan's economy.
Maqbool Sadiq, chairman of the private Karachi Cotton Association, said textile mills had no funds to buy cotton on credit, having already utilised sanctioned loans.
These were authorised on the basis of cotton prices of 1,600 rupees per maund (37.32 kg) last year. With prices now at 2,600 rupees, the mills had used up their credit lines, he added.
This month, the National Credit Consultative Council raised the 1996/97 credit target to 137.1 billion rupees from 102 billion in 1995/96 after a sharp first-half rise.
Domestic credit rose to 128 billion rupees in the first half, compared to a whole-year target of 102 billion.
"Government borrowing for budgetary support alone accounted for well over 60 percent of total credit expansion up to December 26, 1996," an official at the council said.
Money supply had increased five percent, or 47.5 billion rupees, by December 26 compared with the overall target of 116 billion for the whole of 1996/97, the official said.

Lower monetary expansion was the result of a massive depletion of the net foreign assets of the banking system which neutralised to a very large extent the expansionary impact of domestic credit on money supply, he said.
The money supply was now projected to increase to 123 billion rupees, compared to 116 billion rupees originally planned for 1996/97, the official said. ($1 = 40.22 rupees)
